s: Britain's "Atlantis" -- a once-thriving medieval port almost entirely lost to the sea
w: A major medieval port with reportedly eight churches and thousands of residents, swallowed street by street, church by church, as North Sea storms ate the soft cliffs across seven centuries. What remains is a small village and shingle beach; the rest -- harbour, market, graveyards -- lies offshore, and local legend holds that on stormy nights you can still hear the drowned church bells tolling underwater.
_facts: Was a major English port and one of the largest towns in medieval England
Progressively lost to coastal erosion between the 13th and 20th centuries
Most of the original town, including several medieval churches, now lies underwater offshore
Local folklore holds that church bells can be heard ringing beneath the waves during storms

s: the "Island of Secrets" -- a shingle spit of Cold War test sites reclaimed by nature
w: A vast shingle spit reachable only by a National Trust ferry and restricted paths, used through the 20th century for secret aircraft armament, radar and atomic weapons testing. The stark concrete "pagoda" test buildings still stand among rare shingle vegetation and grazing deer, decaying quietly -- one of the more unsettling and singular landscapes on the English coast.
_facts: A 10-mile shingle spit off the Suffolk coast, accessible only by National Trust ferry
Used by the Ministry of Defence for aircraft armament testing, early radar development (from the 1930s) and Cold War-era atomic weapons component testing
Distinctive concrete "pagoda" test buildings remain from the atomic weapons research era
Now a National Trust nature reserve noted for rare shingle habitat and birdlife
